questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?
questions.answer: Physicians expressed concerns about the accuracy of the ambient scribe's drafts, particularly regarding the order of events in the history [1]. They also noted that the confidence underline, designed to highlight potentially inaccurate transcriptions, didn't always effectively address issues with incidental content, such as small talk or irrelevant remarks [2].

sources.title: Interview — Returning Internal Medicine Physician on Edits and Trust Over Time
sources.excerpt:
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, the order of events in the history is where drafts go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, check the sequence of events in the history against the visit, not only word accuracy.
If the team wants to know whether review habits change over time, plan a measure for it; one returning participant's account can't show a trend.

…What I check is whether the story's in the right order." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate)

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Share with the ambient scribe team that the confidence underline doesn't help with incidental content, because that content is usually transcribed accurately; reviewing for it means reading the whole draft.
If anything is designed for this, explore pointing out lines that may not belong in the note rather than removing them, so the clinician makes the call.
Keep this separate from the transcription-confidence work: it is about what belongs in the note, not whether it was heard correctly.
sources.contextBefore:
"It writes down everything that was said, not everything that matters. The sister's surgery is in my note until I take it out." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
"The underline tells me where it wasn't sure what it heard. It heard the small talk perfectly, so nothing tells me to look there." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146
sources.contextAfter:
How often drafts contain incidental content is not measured; "most visits, a line or two" is one physician's impression.
Whether other physicians, NPs and PAs remove the same kinds of content, and how long it takes them, is not known; this is one interview.
What happens to text a clinician removes before signing is not recorded in the corpus and was not discussed in this session.

questions.question: What did coders think of the AI billing code suggestions?
questions.answer: Coders were concerned that AI-assisted coding suggestions could be misconstrued as steering them toward upcoding. [1][2] They wanted explicit documentation that the human coder made the final decision, to avoid the suggestion looking like it steered toward upcoding. [2] They also wanted a visible, per-code record of what was suggested and what the coder did with it (accepted, edited or overridden), which they could see themselves while coding. [3]

sources.title: HIM: Coding, Billing & Release of Information
sources.excerpt: AI-assisted coding suggestions (usability test) surfaced the same underlying concern in a different shape : the senior coder's objection wasn't accuracy (suggestions matched the coder's own independent choice in 14 of 20 test scenarios) but audit posture — they wanted it explicit in the UI and audit log that the human coder made the final call, to avoid the suggestion looking like it steered toward upcoding. This is the same "show your work" / attribution-of-decision pattern seen in prior authorization testing (see [prior-authorization.md](prior-authorization.md)).
sources.contextBefore: …note as Part 2-protected in the EHR — that recurred again independently in the October behavioral health research (see [scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md](scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md)) and was found unchanged in ROI (March 2026) and on the coding side (August 2026), making it a gap confirmed in three threads (ROI, behavioral health and coding) worth fixing regardless of any AI plans.
sources.contextAfter: Recommendation: any AI feature touching this department needs an explicit, audit-log-visible human-decision boundary as a baseline requirement, not a design nicety — this shows up whether the task is redaction, coding, or (per the prior-auth findings) authorization drafting. The 2026 interviews show the boundary is necessary but not sufficient on its own: it has to come with productivity targets…

sources.title: Usability Test — AI-Assisted Medical Coding Suggestions
sources.excerpt:
[HIGH] (compliance risk perception) Senior coder immediately flagged that an AI suggesting codes could be seen as steering toward upcoding if not carefully positioned, and wanted explicit documentation that the human coder made the final call, not the AI, in case of an audit.
[MEDIUM] (accuracy) Suggested codes matched the coder's own independent choice in 14 of 20 test scenarios across participants; mismatches were mostly specificity-level (e.g., unspecified vs. specified diagnosis) rather than category-level.

questions.question: What did the prior auth usability tests find?
questions.answer:
The v1 test found that in 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes [1]. The supervisor in the v1 test said nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here [1]. The v2 test found that the outdated diagnosis code issue did not recur in any of the 4 test cases [2].

The v2 test also found that inline source citations were well-received and used actively — 3 of 4 participants clicked into at least one citation to verify before accepting, which participants described as appropriately fast rather than as friction [2].

questions.question: How was the scribe's draft retention issue resolved?
questions.answer: The draft-retention issue from v0.1 (critical finding, Feb) has been fixed — drafts now auto-expire from the editable state after 10 minutes of inactivity and the behavior is documented for Compliance; verified in all 5 sessions. [1] The draft-ready state's auto-expiry behavior (10 min inactivity) was added directly in response to the 2025-02-25 critical PHI-retention finding. [2] No PHI-handling issues have recurred since. [3]

sources.title: Ambient AI Scribe
sources.excerpt:
The ambient AI scribe has moved from a formative concept (v0.1, Feb 2025) through iteration (v0.2, Sep 2025) to a GA release candidate (Jan 2026). 3 of the original 5 participants returned for v0.2, and at least one (P09) also took part in the GA-candidate round, for longitudinal comparison.
PHI handling: The critical draft-retention/audit gap found in v0.1 was fixed by v0.2 and has remained stable through the GA candidate — drafts auto-expire after 10 minutes of inactivity and the behavior is documented for Compliance. No PHI-handling issues have recurred since.
sources.contextAfter: Accuracy: Medication dosage errors dropped from 3/5 sessions (v0.1) to 1/5 (v0.2); the remaining error type is misheard similar-sounding drug names. The GA-candidate round recommended treating it as a post-GA monitoring item rather than a pre-GA blocker, and recommended a post-GA monitoring dashboard for it; the 2026-02-10 session still refers to that dashboard as recommended.

questions.question: How much drafting time did the AI save on prior auth cases?
questions.answer: The AI cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct [1]. This was confirmed in v2, with time savings measured directly rather than estimated [2].
